'''''Caryota urens''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Arecaceae|palm]] family, native to [[Sri Lanka]], [[India]], [[Myanmar]] and [[Malaysia]] (perhaps elsewhere in [[Malay Archipelago|Indo-Malayan region]]), where they grow in fields and rainforest clearings, it is regarded as introduced in Cambodia.<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 28 March 2020}}</ref><ref name="dyphon">{{cite book |last1=Pauline Dy Phon |title=Plants Used In Cambodia/Plantes utilisées au Cambodge |date=2000 |publisher=Imprimerie Olympic |location=Phnom Penh|page=236|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=InD2RAAACAAJ|author1-link=Pauline Dy Phon }}</ref> The epithet ''urens'' is [[Latin]] for "stinging" alluding to the chemicals in the fruit. Common names in English include '''solitary fishtail palm''', '''kithul palm''', '''toddy palm''', '''wine palm''', '''sago palm''' and '''jaggery palm'''.<ref name=GRIN/> Its leaf is used as fishing rod after trimming the branches of the leaf and drying. According to Monier-Williams, it is called ''moha-karin'' ("delusion maker") in [[Sanskrit]]. It is one of the [[sugar palm]]s.

==Description==
''Caryota urens'' species is a solitary-trunked tree that can measure {{convert|18|m|ft|abbr=off}} in height<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |others=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |page=55 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref> and up to {{convert|30|cm|in|abbr=off}} wide. Widely spaced leaf-scar rings cover its gray trunk which culminate in a {{convert|6|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide, 6 m tall leaf crown. The bipinnate [[leaves]] are triangular in shape, bright to deep green, {{convert|3.5|m|ft|abbr=on}} long, and held on {{convert|60|cm|in|abbr=on}} long [[petiole (botany)|petioles]]. The obdeltoid [[pinnation|pinnae]] are 30 cm long with a pointed edge and a jagged edge.

The {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} long [[inflorescences]] emerge at each leaf node, from top to bottom, producing pendent clusters of white, unisexual [[flowers]]. The [[fruit]] matures to a round, {{convert|1|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=8}} [[drupe]], red in color with one [[seed]]. Like all ''[[Caryotas]]'', the fruit contains [[oxalic acid]], a skin and membrane irritant. As these plants are [[monocarpic]], the completion of the flower and fruiting process results in the death of the tree.

==Uses==
The trunk contains a high quantity of [[starch]] and a juice can be extracted from the shoots of the flowers. The latter can be boiled into a sugary syrup. The cabbage can be eaten raw or cooked.<ref name=":0" />

This species is called '''kithul (කිතුල්)''' in [[Sri Lanka]]. It is best known as the source of kithul treacle, a liquid [[jaggery]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scidev.net/index.cfm?originalUrl=/global/indigenous/feature/sweet-science-sri-lankas-rural-treacle-industry.html&|title=Sweet science: Sri Lanka's rural treacle industry|last=SciDev.Net|website=SciDev.Net}}</ref> The sap of the tree is boiled for many hours until it turns into the thick, dark treacle, unique to Sri Lanka.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Elder|first=Kara|date=June 1, 2021|title=Kithul is Sri Lanka's 'syrup with a funk.' One entrepreneur wants to bring it to the world.|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/food/2021/06/01/kithul-sri-lanka-syrup/}}</ref> Kithul treacle is used as a sweetener in both Sri Lankan and Western cooking.

[[Palm wine|Toddy]] is extracted from the inflorescence, and is considered somewhat powerful compared to toddy extracted from other palm trees. In many parts of  western [[India]] this toddy is fermented and distilled to make a traditional alcohol called as 'Maadi' 

The pulp of the mature plant is cut, sun dried, and powdered, and is edible. It is sweet in taste.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Balachander |first1=Vidya |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2017/01/26/510610923/sri-lankas-kithul-palm-syrup-an-ancient-sweetener-in-need-of-saving|title=Sri Lanka's 'Kithul' Palm Syrup: An Ancient Sweetener In Need Of Saving|website=NPR.org |date=26 January 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.colombotelegraph.com/index.php/kithul-syrup-can-be-sri-lankas-maple-syrup-to-the-world/|title=Kithul Syrup Can Be Sri Lanka's Maple Syrup To The World|date=27 April 2015}}</ref> This powder is considered cool and nutritious in Coastal districts of Karnataka.
In Sri Lanka, the powder is mixed with coconut milk and cooked to make Kithul Thalapa (කිතුල් තලප).

Elephants are fed both the leaf and the pulp of this plant.

The leaves possess strong fibres and are used for basketry in [[Cambodia]], where the plant is named ''tunsaè''.<ref name="dyphon" /> The heart of the trunk contains a starch similar to [[sago]], as well the trunk can be used for building. The fruit, when its stiff hairs are removed, is pleasant and sweet to eat, and, as elsewhere, the Cambodians cut the stalks to make sugar, which in turn can be made into wine.

==Cultivation==
''Caryota urens'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental tree]], and planted in [[garden]]s and parks in tropical and sub-tropical climates. It is also used as an interior and [[houseplant]] when smaller.

==Cultural significance==
On 11 December 2025, the Sri Lankan kithul tapping industry was officially inscribed on [[UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Lists|UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025 |title=Kithul Madeema/Kithul Kapeema, an ancient indigenous technology for tapping Kithul in Sri Lanka - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage |url=https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/kithul-madeema-kithul-kapeema-an-ancient-indigenous-technology-for-tapping-kithul-in-sri-lanka-02318 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251212193637/https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/kithul-madeema-kithul-kapeema-an-ancient-indigenous-technology-for-tapping-kithul-in-sri-lanka-02318 |archive-date=2025-12-12 |access-date=2026-01-12 |website=UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-12-11 |title=Kithul Tapping inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity |url=https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/kithul-tapping-inscribed-unescos-representative-list-intangible-cultural-heritage-humanity |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251214133537/https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/kithul-tapping-inscribed-unescos-representative-list-intangible-cultural-heritage-humanity |archive-date=2025-12-14 |access-date=2026-01-12 |website=UNESCO}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-12-16 |title=Kithul tapping inscribed on UNESCO's representative list |url=https://www.dailymirror.lk/news-features/Kithul-tapping-inscribed-on-UNESCOs-representative-list/131-327928 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260101090906/https://www.dailymirror.lk/news-features/Kithul-tapping-inscribed-on-UNESCOs-representative-list/131-327928 |archive-date=2026-01-01 |access-date=2026-01-12 |website=Daily Mirror |language=en}}</ref>
